title: The Story of Mother Teresa
summary: From a childhood in Skopje to classrooms and care in Calcutta - a story of practical love, prayer, and many helping hands.
coverAlt: Painterly illustration from Mother Teresa's storybook showing young Gonxha and her family in Skopje

pages.title: Gonxha in Skopje
pages.body: In a city called Skopje, a little girl named Gonxha grew up in a loving family. She was born in 1910. Her mother, Drane, taught her to notice people who needed help. When Gonxha was still a child, her father died. Money became tight at home, but her mother kept caring for her children. Gonxha learned that love could be steady even when life was not easy.

pages.title: A Teacher in India
pages.body: As she grew older, she felt drawn to serve God far from home. At eighteen, she left for Ireland to join the Sisters of Loreto. She took the name Sister Teresa, and soon traveled to India. In Calcutta, she taught girls at a school. She prepared lessons, learned from her students, and spent many years in that classroom. Later the other sisters trusted her to lead the school. Teaching children was not a small thing. It was a way to take their minds and their futures seriously.

pages.title: A Call on the Train
pages.body: But Teresa also saw families outside the school who had too little food, safe shelter, or care when they were sick. On a train journey in 1946, she experienced what she later called a "call within a call." She believed Jesus was asking her to serve people who had been pushed aside. This was a prayerful experience she told others about, not a voice everyone on the train heard. She did not simply walk away from her teaching one morning. She brought her wish to Church leaders, prayed, waited, and received permission to begin something new.

pages.title: Learning to Care
pages.body: In 1948, Teresa left the Loreto convent wearing a simple white sari with a blue border. Before beginning her work, she spent time learning basic medical care. She went into the neighborhoods of Calcutta to visit families, teach children who had no classroom, and care for people who were sick. Her hands could wash a wound. Her words could ask someone how they were. Neither kindness nor prayer meant leaving a sick person without care. She learned practical skills because love needed to reach the whole person.

pages.title: Others Join Her
pages.body: Picture a room where a child is learning letters, while outside neighbors are finding help for someone who is ill. That picture gathers together different parts of her work; it is not one recorded afternoon. Teresa could not mend every hurt in the city by herself. Still, she could meet the person in front of her, and others could join her. Former students and new sisters came to help. In 1950, the Church formally established their community, the Missionaries of Charity. They promised a life of prayer and service to people many others overlooked.

pages.title: Many Hands at Work
pages.body: The sisters' work grew beyond one neighborhood and then beyond India. Together with co-workers of different backgrounds, they cared for people who were hungry, sick, or lonely. Teresa became known around the world. In 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize. A prize did not mean all suffering had ended, and it did not make one person the answer to every problem. It drew attention to the dignity of the people she served and to the work that many hands were doing.

pages.title: When Prayer Felt Dark
pages.body: There was something most people did not know while she was alive. In her private letters, Teresa wrote about long stretches when she could not feel God close to her. She kept praying, and she kept serving, even when prayer felt dark. Children sometimes wonder whether a hard feeling means they have done something wrong. It does not. Teresa's story does not ask anyone to hide pain or refuse help. It shows that love can remain a choice even on days when the heart does not feel strong.

pages.title: A Saint Remembered
pages.body: She died in Calcutta in 1997. Years later, in 2016, the Church proclaimed her a saint. Catholics honor her because she kept turning toward Jesus in people the world could overlook. Her story is not a promise that one kind act will solve another person's troubles. It is an invitation to see a person first, ask what they need, and take a useful step with them.

pages.title: Who Is Before You?
pages.body: What might that look like for you? Maybe you notice a child left out of a game, or help someone carry a bag, or tell a trusted grown-up when a neighbor needs more help than you can give. You do not have to travel far, win a prize, or fix everything alone. You can pray for eyes that notice people, hands ready to help, and the humility to ask others to join you. Mother Teresa began with the person before her. Who is before you today?

pages.title: Points of reflection
pages.body:
First, Teresa noticed people who were easy to pass by. Jesus taught his followers to love their neighbors. Who around you might need to be seen and heard today?

Second, she learned how to help, not only how to feel sorry. Love can mean doing the useful thing: asking what someone needs, sharing your time, or getting a trusted adult when the problem is bigger than you.

Third, she welcomed others into the work. God calls us to care for one another; no one has to fix the world alone. Who could you invite to do one kind thing with you?

Fourth, she kept praying and caring even when she could not feel God near. A hard day is not a failure of faith. What small prayer, honest conversation, or request for help could carry you through a hard day?

Think of one person and one kind step you can take this week. Ask God for the courage to take it, and remember to listen to what that person actually needs.
